The paper addresses steady-state Maxwell's equations for electromagnetic absorption and scattering problems.
A weak formulation using a Lagrange multiplier is introduced to enforce the divergence (Gauss) condition.
The hp-adaptive finite element method allows local variation of element size h and polynomial order p.
The method supports curved finite elements to model complex geometries.
Stability and convergence are proven for affine elements with polynomial shape functions.
The formulation is stable uniformly with respect to frequency, including as frequency approaches zero.
The Lagrange multiplier is sometimes called a dummy variable since it vanishes at the continuous level.
The model problem involves two media with different material constants separated by an interface with jump conditions.
Boundary conditions include perfect electric conductor and magnetic symmetry wall conditions.
The reduced wave equation for the electric field is derived by eliminating the magnetic field.
Finite element spaces are constructed with polynomial orders varying per element and per edge.
Scalar and vector finite element spaces satisfy a compatibility condition ensuring stability.
The method is motivated by applications in mixed digital-analog signal packages and human body electromagnetic modeling.
Numerical experiments include 2D cases with curved boundaries and nonhomogeneous media.
The eigenvalue problem associated with the curl-curl operator has zero eigenvalue of infinite multiplicity and positive eigenvalues tending to infinity.
The stability constant depends on the frequency and eigenvalues but remains bounded away from resonance frequencies.
The method can handle discontinuous material properties and singular solutions effectively.
The paper provides explicit formulas for the dimension of finite element spaces with variable polynomial orders.
The finite element shape functions include vertex, mid-side, and middle nodes with associated Lagrangian degrees of freedom.
The global continuity of scalar and vector approximations is enforced by sharing degrees of freedom at element interfaces.
